draft.plain:
This is a made-up practice document about a pottery or craft workshop run by Marigold Bench Studio. Here is what it says in plain language.

THE PRICE AND PAYMENTS
The full price is $240. You pay $60 now as a deposit. That $60 is part of the $240 — not extra on top. You pay the remaining $180 no later than seven calendar days before January 24, 2027 at 10:00 UTC.

IF YOU CANCEL FIVE DAYS BEFORE THE EVENT
Five days before the event is fewer than seven calendar days before the start. That means your cancellation arrives too late for a refund. The rule says: cancellations received fewer than seven calendar days before the start are non-refundable. So if you cancel five days before, you would get nothing back — unless the Studio itself cancels (see below).

IF THE STUDIO CANCELS
If the Studio cancels the workshop, you get every penny back — the $60 deposit, the $180 balance, and even the $12 booking fee. This override applies no matter when the Studio cancels, and it beats both of the normal cancellation rules.

IF BAD WEATHER STOPS YOU GOING
Bad weather alone does not qualify for the special full-refund override. The document says so directly. This means bad weather on its own falls under the normal cancellation rules — and since you would be cancelling fewer than seven days before the event, that would be non-refundable. The document does not give you a separate weather refund right.

IF AN OFFICIAL EVACUATION ORDER STOPS YOU GOING
An official evacuation order that actually prevents you from reaching the venue on the day of the event does qualify for a full refund, including the $12 booking fee. But two conditions must both be true: (1) there must be an official evacuation order — not just bad weather or a personal choice — and (2) you must give the Studio written notice before the scheduled start time of 10:00 UTC on January 24, 2027. If you miss that deadline or only have bad weather (not an evacuation order), this override does not apply.

THE $12 BOOKING FEE
Normally, even a timely cancellation (seven or more days before) costs you a $12 booking fee — it is kept by the Studio and not refunded. Only the Studio-cancels override and the evacuation-order override give you that $12 back.

HOW REFUNDS ARE PAID
Once you make a valid refund request, the Studio has ten business days to pay you. Business days usually means working days, not weekends or public holidays, but the document does not define this further.

REMINDER: This is a fictional test document. It is not a real offer or agreement.

affectsYou.point: Cancelling five days before the event gets you nothing back. Five days is fewer than seven calendar days, so the non-refundable rule applies — you would lose the full $240 you paid, unless the Studio itself cancels.

Bad weather alone does not trigger a refund. The document specifically excludes bad weather from the evacuation override, and a late cancellation for any other reason is also non-refundable. So bad weather on its own leaves you with no refund right under this document.
An evacuation order gives you a full refund — but only if you send written notice to the Studio before 10:00 UTC on January 24, 2027. Miss that deadline and you lose the right to this override.
If the Studio cancels, you get everything back including the $12 booking fee. This is the strongest protection in the document and overrides all other rules.
The remaining $180 is due seven calendar days before January 24, 2027 at 10:00 UTC. If you miss that payment, the document does not say what happens — that is a gap worth asking about.
Any refund is paid within ten business days of a valid refund request. The document does not define 'business days' or say how to submit a refund request, so it is worth confirming the process.

questions: If I cancel exactly seven calendar days before the 10:00 UTC start — does my written cancellation need to arrive before 10:00 UTC on that day to count as 'at least seven days', or is the whole day acceptable?
What counts as 'written notice' for an evacuation-order refund claim — is an email enough, or do you require a specific form or method?
What happens if I have not paid the $180 balance by the seven-day deadline — do I lose my place, lose my deposit, or is there a grace period?
If there is an official evacuation order but it is lifted before 10:00 UTC on January 24, 2027, would I still qualify for the evacuation refund?
How do I submit a refund request, and does the ten-business-day clock start from when I send the request or when you receive and approve it?

draft.plain:
This is a fictional contract document for an invented service called Fable Harbor Workspace, a project-board subscription. It is not a real service or real legal agreement. Here is what the terms say:

**What you're subscribing to and what it costs**
The subscription costs $30 per month. It renews automatically every month.

**How to cancel**
You must cancel before 23:59 UTC on the calendar day before your next billing date. That is the cutoff — not midnight on your billing date, but the night before. If you cancel in time, the next charge does not happen, and you keep access until the end of the period you already paid for.

**Refunds for cancellation**
If you cancel mid-month, you do not get a refund for the unused days. The document says payments are not refunded simply because you cancel early. However, there is one specific exception: if you were charged twice for the same thing (a duplicate charge), the duplicate amount is refunded in full — but only if you report it within 30 calendar days of that charge.

**What the provider is liable for if something goes wrong — the general cap**
If the provider makes an ordinary mistake that causes you harm, the most they owe you is the total subscription fees you actually paid during the three months before you make your claim. At $30 per month, that would be up to $90 if you paid $30 each of those three months — but the actual cap depends on what you actually paid in that period, not a fixed $90.

**When the general cap does not apply**
The three-month cap is lifted in two specific situations: (1) fraud by the provider, and (2) unauthorized disclosure of your confidential documents. In those two cases, the provider cannot hide behind the cap. However, lifting the cap does not automatically mean you can recover everything — the lost-profits exclusion is a separate rule that still applies on its own terms (see below).

**Lost profits — a separate and important rule**
The document has a separate rule about lost profits (money your business loses because of the provider's actions). By default, you cannot recover lost profits at all. There is only one exception: you can recover lost profits if they were directly caused by the provider's fraud. That is the only override.

This means: if the provider makes an ordinary service mistake, you cannot recover lost profits. If the provider commits an unauthorized disclosure of your confidential documents — even though that lifts the liability cap — you still cannot recover lost profits, because unauthorized disclosure alone is not an exception to the lost-profits exclusion. The document states this explicitly. Only fraud that directly causes your lost profits opens the door to recovering them.

To be clear about how these two rules interact: beating the liability cap (because of fraud or unauthorized disclosure) does not automatically beat the lost-profits exclusion. Those are two separate hurdles. You need to clear each one independently.

affectsYou.point: Lost profits from an unauthorized disclosure of your design files are not recoverable. Even though unauthorized disclosure lifts the liability cap, the lost-profits exclusion still applies separately and is not overridden by that exception. If a leak of your confidential design work causes clients to cancel contracts with your studio, you likely cannot recover those lost profits under these terms.

Lost profits are only recoverable if directly caused by the provider's fraud. For your studio, this matters most: if the provider's fraud directly causes you to lose client contracts or revenue, you can claim those lost profits. But for any other type of harm — ordinary mistakes or even unauthorized disclosure — lost profits are off the table.

For ordinary service mistakes (not fraud, not unauthorized disclosure), the most you can recover is the subscription fees you actually paid in the three months before your claim. At $30/month, that is up to $90 if you paid $30 each of those three months — but the actual cap depends on your actual payment history in that period. If a service outage disrupts your studio's project delivery, your compensation is capped at that amount, and lost profits are excluded entirely.

You must cancel before 23:59 UTC the calendar day before your next billing date to avoid being charged again. If you miss that cutoff by even a minute, you will be billed for another month. There are no refunds for cancelling mid-month, so timing your cancellation precisely matters for your studio's budget.

If you are ever charged twice in the same billing cycle, you can get the duplicate amount refunded in full — but you must report it within 30 calendar days of that charge. Missing that window means losing the right to that refund.

The liability cap does not apply to fraud or unauthorized disclosure of your confidential documents. For a design studio, your confidential project files and client work could qualify as confidential documents, so this exception is relevant — but remember, lifting the cap does not by itself let you recover lost profits.

questions: What exactly counts as 'confidential documents' under this agreement — would my client briefs, design files, and unreleased concepts be covered, and what security measures protect them from unauthorized disclosure?
If I cancel the day before my billing date, what timezone should I use to confirm the 23:59 UTC cutoff, and is there a confirmation I receive so I have proof I cancelled in time?

If an unauthorized disclosure of my studio's design work causes me to lose a client contract, is there any path to recovering those lost profits, or does the lost-profits exclusion apply absolutely in that scenario?
How do you define 'fraud' for the purpose of the lost-profits exception — what would I need to show to prove that my lost profits were directly caused by your fraud?
If I believe I have a claim, what is the process for making it, and is there a deadline by which I must bring a claim after the harm occurs?

draft.plain:
This is a fictional warranty document for a Cobalt Fern label printer. Here is what it says in plain English.

The warranty lasts twelve months from the day the printer is delivered. It covers manufacturing defects — meaning problems that came from how the printer was built — and it includes both parts and labor. If a defect is found, Cobalt Fern decides whether to repair or replace the printer; you do not get to choose.

Three things are excluded: damage from dropping the printer, damage from liquid exposure, and damage caused by a third-party repair. That third exclusion is important for you: because someone other than Cobalt Fern previously repaired a roller, any damage that was caused by that repair is not covered. However, the warranty is not cancelled entirely. Manufacturing defects that are unrelated to the third-party repair remain covered. Whether your ink cartridge leak is related to the roller repair is not something this document decides — that causal link is uncertain and would need to be assessed during inspection.

There is a specific exception for liquid damage: if the leak came from the original factory-installed ink cartridge and that cartridge's original tamper seal is still intact at the time of the failure, the liquid damage is covered despite the general liquid-damage exclusion. Refilled cartridges do not qualify for this exception. Based on what you have described — an original factory-installed cartridge with its tamper seal intact — your situation appears to match the conditions for this exception, but Cobalt Fern would need to confirm that during inspection.

Return shipping: You pay the return shipping cost upfront. If Cobalt Fern confirms a manufacturing defect, they will reimburse your documented return shipping costs up to $20. If no defect is confirmed, the shipping cost is not reimbursed.

Inspection fee: A $35 fee applies only if two conditions are both true — no manufacturing defect is found, AND you agreed to that fee in writing before the inspection took place. If you did not consent in writing beforehand, the document does not authorize Cobalt Fern to charge you the $35 fee, even if no defect is found. The document does not describe any other charges.

This document does not cover refunds, cancellations, or any other financial arrangements beyond what is described above.

affectsYou.point: Your ink cartridge leak may be covered. The document has a specific exception: liquid damage from a leak in the original factory-installed ink cartridge is covered if the original tamper seal is intact when the failure happens. You have described exactly that situation. However, Cobalt Fern must confirm this during inspection — coverage is not automatic.

The third-party roller repair creates a partial risk. Damage caused by that repair is excluded. The document does not say the roller repair caused the cartridge leak, and that causal link is uncertain — but Cobalt Fern could argue the leak was caused by the prior repair. If they make that finding, the liquid-damage exception would not help you and the claim could be denied.

You must pay return shipping upfront. If a manufacturing defect is confirmed, Cobalt Fern reimburses documented return shipping costs up to $20. Keep your receipt. If no defect is confirmed, you are not reimbursed for shipping at all.

A $35 inspection fee can only be charged if no defect is found AND you agreed to it in writing before the inspection. Do not sign or consent to that fee in writing unless you understand that doing so authorizes the charge if no defect is found. If you have not yet consented in writing, the document does not authorize Cobalt Fern to charge you this fee.
Cobalt Fern chooses repair or replacement — not you. If your claim is approved, you cannot demand a specific remedy. The document does not promise any particular service timeline either.

questions: Will you inspect the tamper seal on the original factory-installed ink cartridge first, and confirm in writing whether it qualifies for the liquid-damage exception before any other assessment takes place?

If you find that the cartridge leak qualifies for the liquid-damage exception, will you also assess whether the third-party roller repair is related to the cartridge failure — and how will you document that finding?
Before I send the printer in, will you confirm in writing whether you are asking me to consent to the $35 inspection fee, and what happens if I do not consent?
What documentation do you require for me to be reimbursed for return shipping, and how and when will that reimbursement be paid if a defect is confirmed?
